coredata.dc:title: The effect of shock loads on the performance of an anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR). 1. Step changes in feed concentration at constant retention time
coredata.dc:creator: Nachaiyasit, Suyanee
Stuckey, David C.
coredata.dc:description: A 10-litre anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR), with eight compartments, was used to examine the effect of organic shock loads, in the form of a step change in the feed chemical oxygen demand (COD) at constant hydraulic retention time (HRT), on reactor performance in terms of COD removal, and to obtain a greater insight into microbial responses and interactions during these shocks. In order to minimise feed variations, and have a totally biodegradable substrate, a synthetic carbohydrate (sucrose)-protein (meat extract) substrate was used. The reactor was operated at 20-h HRT, 4 g/litre COD (4.8 kg-COD/m3 d), and 35°C for 1 month as a base-line condition, and this resulted in 98% COD removal. It was found that a step change in the feed to 8 g/litre COD (9.6 kg-COD/m3 d) at 20-h HRT for 20 days did not affect the substrate removal efficiency at all; however, when the concentration was increased to 15 g/litre COD (18 kg-COD/m3 d) from 4 g/litre for 20 days, the removal efficiency decreased to 90%. It was found that the compartmentalised ABR consisted of three general zones (acidification, methanation, and a buffer zone where little acidification and methanogenesis occurs), and the function of high solids concentrations in the reactor was to enhance stability rather than improve COD removal. Hence, the structure of the ABR prevents most of the biomass being exposed to low pHs during shock loads, and enhances reactor stability. In addition, due to low pHs and high substrate concentrations in the first compartment, a microbial population seems to be selected which produces primarily acetate and butyrate rather than formate and propionate, and this also enhances the stability of the reactor during shock loads. In contrast to past results, formate did not seem to be an important interspecies electron carrier except under high mixing conditions and shock loads, and this was postulated to be due to differences in the structure of the microbial flocs. Based on these observations, the ABR holds some promise as a reactor design for anaerobic industrial wastewater treatment.

STEP CHANGES IN FEED CONCENTRATION AT CONSTANT RETENTION TIME SUYANEE NACHAIYASIT and DAVID C. STUCKEY@* Department of Chemical Engineering and Chemical Technology, Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine, Prince Consort Road, London, SW7 2BY, U.K. (Received June 1996, accepted in revised form April 1997) Abstract--A 10-1itre anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR), with eight compartments, was used to examine the effect of organic shock loads, in the form of a step change in the feed chemical oxygen demand (COD) at constant hydraulic retention time (HRT), on reactor performance in terms of COD removal, and to obtain a greater insight into microbial responses and interactions during these shocks. In order to minimise feed variations, and have a totally biodegradable substrate, a synthetic carbohydrate (sucrose)-protein (meat extract) substrate was used. The reactor was operated at 20-h HRT, 4g/litre COD (4.8 kg-COD/m3 d), and 35 for 1 month as a base-line condition, and this resulted in 98% COD removal. It was found that a step change in the feed to 8 g/litre COD (9.6 kg-COD/m3 d) at 20-h HRT for 20 days did not affect the substrate removal efficiency at all; however, when the concentration was increased to 15 g/litre COD (18 kg-COD/m3 d) from 4 g/litre for 20 days, the removal efficiency decreased to 90%. It was found that the compartmentalised ABR consisted of three general zones (acidification, methanation, and a buffer zone where little acidification and methanogenesis occurs), and the function of high solids concentrations in the reactor was to enhance stability rather than improve COD removal. Hence, the structure of the ABR prevents most of the biomass being exposed to low pHs during shock loads, and enhances reactor stability. In addition, due to low pHs and high substrate concentrations in the first compartment, a microbial population seems to be selected which produces primarily acetate and butyrate rather than formate and propionate, and this also enhances the stability of the reactor during shock loads. In contrast to past results, formate did not seem to be an important interspecies electron carrier except under high mixing conditions and shock loads, and this was postulated to be due to differences in the structure of the microbial flocs. Based on these observations, the ABR holds some promise as a reactor design for anaerobic industrial wastewater treatment. 1997 Elsevier Science Ltd Key words--anaerobic baffled reactor, anaerobic digestion, organic shock loads, interspecies electron transfer, volatile acids ratio INTRODUCTION The anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR) has been described as a series of UASBs which does not require granulation for its operation (Bachmann et al., 1985). This design consists of a series of vertical baffles which force the wastewater to flow under and over them as it passes from the inlet to the outlet (Fig. 1). The bacteria tend to rise and settle with gas production in each compartment, but they move horizontally down the reactor at a relatively slow rate giving rise to cell retention times (CRT) of 100 days at 20-h hydraulic retention time (HRT) (Grobicki and Stuckey, 1991). The wastewater can, therefore, come into intimate contact with a large amount of *Author to whom all correspondence should be addressed [Tel: +0171-594 5591, Fax: +0171-594 5604, E-mail: d.stuckey@ic.ac.uk]. active biomass as it passes through the ABR with short HRTs (6-20h), while the effluent remains relatively free of biological solids. This configuration has been shown to result in a high degree of chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal (Grobicki and Stuckey, 1991). Because of the variable nature of industrial wastes, reactor stability to organic shock loads is one of the most important aspects of reactor design. These shock loads can manifest themselves in two ways: either as a short-term transient which only lasts a few hours, or as a longer-term step change of days to weeks before reversion back to the original operating conditions. In the first few hours to days, the microbial response to both these shock loads are identical; however, the longer-term shock leads to a new "steady state" which may or may not be identical to the original operating conditions in terms of COD removal and other parameters. In high CRT reactors such as the ABR, in contrast to completely stirred 2737 2738 S. Nachaiyasit and D. C. Stuckey tank reactors (CSTRs), the time required to establish a new steady state after a step change is considerably longer than the accepted norm of three HRTs, and little is known about the dynamic changes the microbial populations undergo in the transition from one steady state to another. Over the years a number of workers have looked at the effect of organic shock loads on anaerobic reactors; some of these have been brief transients, while others were longer term shocks. Barnes et al. (1983) examined the response of an anaerobic fluidised bed to shock loads of a high biological oxygen demand (BOD) synthetic feed (keeping HRT constant) imposed over a period of 1 hour. Borja et al. (1994) subjected an anaerobic downflow filter at 35 treating slaughterhouse wastewater with a feed concentration of 5050 mg-COD/litre to a 100 and 150% increase in influent COD for 5-h and 10-h periods by adding a blood solution. A feed containing acetic acid plus nutrients at 35 was used to study the response of a reactor to continuous operation with step changes in feed concentration which varied from 50 to 200% of the steady-state feed level of 12,000 mg/litre (Carr and O'Donnell, 1977). Arcand et al. (1994) found that increasing specific loading rates from low to high significantly increased the proportion of postacidogenic bacteria (a generic term to denote all bacteria involved in butyrate, propionate, acetate, and hydrogen catabolism, i.e. non-acidogenic bacteria) at the expense of acidogens in an upflow anaerobic sludge bed and filter system reactor treating a synthetic sugar wastewater at 35. In summary, the general response of anaerobic processes to an organic shock can be characterised by the following: an increase in volatile fatty acids (VFAs); a decrease in removal efficiency; a decrease in methane content, but an increase in methane production; higher effluent suspended solids (SS); an increase in the sludge volume index; an increase in the proportion of postacidogenic bacteria; and an increased or decreased pH depending on the buffer capacity of the influent and the system (Mathiot et al., 1992; Borja et al., 1994). Consequently, the highest concentration shock load causes the lengthi- est deterioration of effluent quality in terms of peak soluble COD (BOD) and VFA concentrations (Barnes et al., 1983). This increase in soluble COD in the effluent will consist of both unmetabolised VFAs and soluble microbial products (SMPs) (Noguera et al., 1994). The degree of deterioration in performance depends on the duration and magnitude of the shock and the rate of adaptability of the microbes; hence, the function of higher biomass concentrations in anaerobic reactors is usually to enhance their stability rather than improve COD removal. In terms of understanding the effect of shock loads on key intermediates in the ABR, the concept of interspecies electron transport, with the concomitant close physical association of electron producing and electron consuming bacteria (Guiot et al., 1990), is important. The discovery that syntrophic methanogenic reactions were compartmentalised within the flocs by species juxtapositioning was a key finding and has been noted in the ABR (Grobicki and Stuckey, 1991), and demonstrated by electron microscope analysis of various granules (Alphenaar et al., 1993). However, in some cases, mass transfer may become a problem due to the small concen- tration gradients. Dolfing (1992) estimated that a 20% decrease in the hydrogen concentration in the range of 10-100nM would result in a 25-31% decrease in the energy flux through methanogens in the typical conditions encountered in methanogenic aggregates. One mechanism of interspecies electron transfer which may overcome these mass-transfer problems is via formate, although this subject is still controversial (Thiele et al., 1988). Boone et al. (1989) calculated the potential moles of hydrogen and formate diffusing in a dispersed cell butyrate-degrading co-culture and Biogas Influent Liquid supernat~ Sludge bed flluent 50 Fig. 1. Thus, interspecies formate transfer was considered to be the predominant mechanism in the syntrophic association. However, Bieicher and Winter (1994) urged that the concept of interspecies formate transfer be reconsidered, since, in pure cultures of methanogens or complex ecosystems with excess hydrogen, formate formation seemed to serve more as a means of disposal of surplus reducing power. Nevertheless, an early study on the ABR (Grobicki and Stuckey, 1991) found that, in reactors containing 6-11 g-VSS/litre of biomass present in the form of granules, even at steady state with a 4 g/litre feed and an HRT of 20 h, formate levels as high as 4200mg/litre were measured in compartment 1. However, this reduced to 800 mg/litre in compart- ment 2, and, as the HRT decreased to 5 h, the concentration in compartment 1 decreased substan- tially. In contrast, others have suggested that formate transfer is not necessary in anaerobic digestion (Dornseiffer et al., 1995). Despite the above contradictions, a comment on the relative importance of hydrogen and formate by Stams (1994) may summarise the current situation best: "In syntrophic cultures both the hydrogen and formate concen- trations are extremely low, and it is difficult to deduce which of the two is most important. However, in methanogenic granular sludge, interspecies hydrogen transfer might be most important .... while there is evidence to support the fact that formate might be more important than hydrogen transfer in suspended culture". Due to the partial separation of trophic groups in the ABR, shock loads may also provide insights into microbial responses and interactions under a variety of environmental conditions. McCarty and Mosey (1991) suggested that the relative ratios of reduced end-products produced by the catabolism of carbo- hydrates were controlled more by population dynamics as a result of competition between bacteria producing propionic and butyric acid under varying substrate concentrations and pH, rather than through the concentration of hydrogen in the system controlling the kinetics and thermodynamics of catabolism. This hypothesis is extremely relevant to the ABR, since the ratio of VFAs produced in the first compartment is controlled by feed COD and HRT (via pH and substrate concentration), and hence this compartment determines the feed compo- sition to the rest of the reactor, and possibly its response to shock loads. Hence, the objective of this work was to investigate the stability of the ABR to step changes in organic feed concentrations (COD) at constant HRT over a period of time until the reactor had reached steady state, and to monitor key intermediates in order to obtain a greater insight into microbial responses and interactions during these shocks. MATERIALS AND METHODS Two reactors were set up, each with a working volume of l0 litres and consisting of eight separate compartments of equal volume; details of the reactors can be found in Grobicki and Stuckey (199 l). The reactors were maintained at a constant temperature of 35 +_ 0.5 in a water-bath. The effluent line contained a glass U-tube for level control and to trap biomass before running to an effluent reservoir. There was one feed stream to each reactor, pumped by a variable-speed peristaltic pump. In order to avoid problems with varying composition and degradability of the feed, a buffered synthetic carbohydrate-protein substrate was used supplemented with nutrients and trace metals (Nachaiyasit and Stuckey, 1995). CH4 and CO_, were monitored by GC-TCD (coefficient of variation, CV = %), while H2 concentrations were measured by a GMI meter (CV = + 1%). The total gas production was monitored using gas-water displacement over an acidified salt solution to prevent CO_, absorption. The concentration of volatile acids (formate, acetate, propionate and butyrate) and glucose in each compartment was quantified by HPLC (CV--1%), and separation was achieved after centrifugation for 15 min at 9000 rpm, with an ion-exchange resin column (ION-300 series, 300 x 7.8 mm, Alltech) using l0 mM H2SO4 at 0.5 ml/min, and the concentrations were measured at 215 nm. Glucose concentrations were monitored with an RI detector, and since the feed sucrose was hydrolysed to equimolar amounts of both glucose and fructose which were eluted at similar times, and degraded at similar rates, only glucose was reported in the data presented. Conventional parameters such as pH, COD, alkalinity and solids concentrations (total and volatile) were monitored as required by standard methods (APHA, 1989). The reactors were initially started with an inoculum of 10 litres of screened digested sludge (total solids 30 g/litre, volatile solids 18 g/litre), and then operated for 2 years to assess the effect of effluent recycle and low temperatures on reactor performance. The reactors were then operated for I month with a feed COD of 4 g/litre and HRT of 20 h at 35 to provide a steady baseline for this study. Reactor II was then selected and the feed concentration changed to 8 g/litre for 20 days at an HRT of 20 h while various parameters were monitored and steady state reached (defined by constant COD values in the effluent for 4 days). The feed was then changed back to 4 g/litre for 30 days to allow the reactor to reach its baseline performance again. Finally, the feed strength was increased in error to 13 g/litre for l15h before being increased to 15g/litres, and the reactor was monitored to steady state. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Data at an HRT of 20 h on the variations of COD, hydrogen, pH, and VFA/glucose levels over 202 h after a feed concentration step change from 4 to 8 g-COD/litre, and over 312 h after a change from 4 to 15g-COD/litre are shown below. Finally, a summary of reactor performance at steady state after each change is presented. The behaviour of the parameters was as follows. COD. From Figure 2, it can be seen that, as the shock wave moved down the reactor, the size of the COD peaks decreased; however, 2 days after the shock the peaks had flattened out at higher levels from time zero in compartments 1 and 2, and slightly greater levels in compartments 3 and 4. This was probably the net result of increased substrate concentrations which increased the substrate flux into the bioaggregates, thereby increasing the growth rate of the internal microbes (mostly acetogens and methanogens). This led to an enhanced removal rate of intermediates to methane, the production of more gas, enhanced mixing (more even distribution of the substrate amongst the microbes) and, consequently, after 2 days, lower levels of COD. It may be concluded from this data that, even with a doubling of the load, the reactor was stable and responded rapidly to the shock. It was interesting to note that in this case the ABR reached a new steady state quite rapidly, and the time required was equivalent to a CSTR, i.e. approximately three HRTs (~60 h). Hydrogen. From Fig. 3, it can be seen that there was hardly any change in the hydrogen levels of compartments 4 to 8, while the activity of hydrogen metabolism (production and utilisation) was high in the first two compartments and, to a lesser extent, in compartment 3. This is evidence of an active acidification zone in the first few compartments of the reactor and a rapid turnover of hydrogen. pH. From Fig. 4, it is apparent that the pH levels initially rose and then dropped rapidly and dramatically in compartments 1 and 2, stayed relatively constant in compartment 3 and increased in compartments 4 to 8. The decrease in pH in compartments 1 and 2 was the result of VFAs building up, while the increases in compartments 4 to 8 were due to the increased buffering capacity with increased feed concentration, and the efficient conversion of intermediates to methane at high loads in the middle zone of the reactor. In contrast to the ABR, Carr and O'Donnell (1977) showed that in a CSTR a step change of 100% in the feed was on the borderline between recovery and failure, and the result depended on the initial solids levels in the digester. Formate was only present at low concentrations in the first 13 h and only showed a slight increase thereafter, but it never climbed beyond 200 mg/litre. This increase in formate could be due to either of the following: an increase in formate production; an elevated degree of mixing leading to a release of some of the formate from the flocs; a decrease in formate utilisation; or a combination of all three. However, this observation is in direct contrast to some of the authors' earlier work (Grobicki and Stuckey, 1991), where with essentially the same feed (except that the alkalinity was 30% higher in this study and trace metals were added), even under steady-state con- ditions, formate levels as high as 4200 mg/litre were measured in the first compartment. At this point it is difficult to explain this observation, but since .the biomass concentrations in the earlier work were 3-4 times lower and granules were present, it appears that this difference was probably due to the different structure of the bioaggregates and lower pHs in the first two compartments, and this observation highlights the importance of the physical nature of the association of the biomass. The ratio of acetate/butyrate after the feed change varied from 2.2 to 2.8, compared to a ratio of 3.2 at time zero. This observation appears to confirm McCarty and Mosey's (1991) hypothesis that at lower pHs butyrate production, in contrast to formate, acetate or propionate, is favoured, and an increased production of butyrate instead of acetate might be one way that microbial consortia combat high acidity. After 2 clays the levels of acetate and butyrate decreased, while propionate always stayed below 300 mg/litre (a small increase from time zero) and did not exceed the butyrate level. When considering the profile of VFAs in compartment 2 (Fig. 6), it can be seen that no glucose was detected (all consumed), and there was considerably higher levels of acetate and lower levels of butyrate in this compartment compared to compartment 1. This could have been the result of lower levels of hydrogen in compartment 2, which would allow the conversion of butyrate into acetate. In addition, the bulk pH values in compartment 2 were slightly higher than in compartment 1, leading to lower butyrate production. The average values of propionate in this compartment were higher than that of compartment 1; however, they never exceeded 400 mg/litre. Despite being below 400 mg/litre, the level of propionate in compartment 3 was greater than the butyrate level, and this persisted with declining concentrations until compartment 6 (results not shown). The persistence of propionate may be attributable to the small number of propionate utilisers (only two species of syntrophs are known to degrade propionate, and they have the slowest growth rates of the acid utilising group--Houwen et al., 1990). VFA levels decreased in successive compartments, especially from compartment 4 onwards, and this explains the increase in pH in these compartments together with the increasing alkalinity. Finally, there were very low levels of acetate and propionate detected in compartment 6, and none was found in compartments 7 and 8. However, the COD level never quite decreased to zero (80 mg/litre-- Fig. 2), due to SMPs being released during catabolism and cell lysis. Every compartment stabilised after some time at higher levels of COD, hydrogen, VFAs and pH. After day 4 (hour 96) the feed concentration was stepped up from 13 to 15 g-COD/litre, and this resulted in higher bulk CODs and hydrogen levels but hardly any change in the pH trend. The behaviour of the system parameters was as follows. COD. Figure 7 shows the rapid change in COD that occurred within a day after the change in feed strength, and these values remained high even after 13 days. However, when the COD levels in all the compartments are considered, the increase was greatest in the first compartment and was dampened down along the reactor. The increase in COD was the result of a rapid rate of VFA production and a slower rate of utilisation by the methanogens. Despite this increase, it can be seen that the COD removal in the first compartment still amounted to around 3000 mg/ litre, presumably due to the rapid conversion of hydrogen to methane. In contrast to the 8 g/litre shock, the ABR was still undergoing changes even after 13 days (15 HRTs) and had not come to steady state, demonstrating the effect of the slow growth rate of methanogens. Hydrogen. Compared with the level of hydrogen during the 8 g/litre shock, it can be seen that, during the 15 g/litre shock, the hydrogen produced was considerably higher in compartments 1 and 2 and greatly exceeded the maximum level of the hydrogen sensor (2000 ppm) (Fig. 8). By extrapolating these profiles it appears that the hydrogen levels could have exceeded 10,000ppm. However, even these levels decreased after 8-10 days, and this was undoubtedly due to the rapid growth of hydrogen utilisers. It is interesting to note that, even under such large organic shocks, hydrogen production and utilisation still only occurs primarily in the first two compartments of the ABR. The spike in compartment 3 (and 4/5) at 115 h was due to the feed concentration being increased from 13 to 15 g/litre. pH. The pH increased rapidly after time zero in every compartment in spite of the higher levels of COD (VFA accumulation), and this was probably due to the effect of the high buffering capacity of the feed. In this study the alkalinity of the influent and the effluent were 6500 and 6750 mg/litre, respectively, at steady state with 15 g/litre, compared to 3600 and 4500 mg/litre at steady state with 8 g/litre and 1800 and 2200 mg/litre under normal operating conditions with a 4 g/litre feed concentration (Fig. 9). In compartment I (Fig. 10) glucose increased rapidly to a concentration of around 40% of the feed concentration (5265 mg/litre) after only 24 h. This clearly demonstrates that the acidogens were considerably overloaded at this feed concen- tration. Formate increased after the shock but did not reach very high levels (less than 700 mg/litre), and this could have been the result of increased mixing at higher gas productions, releasing more formate from the biofloc, or serving as a means of disposal of surplus reducing power. The levels of acetate in this compartment were not high compared to those in compartment 2, and this was probably due to the incomplete conversion of the feed. However, com- pared to the 8 g/litre shock, greater amounts of glucose (2800-200 = 2600 mg/litre in 8 g/litre, com- pared to 5265-2200 = 3025mg/litre in 15 g/litre) were consumed in the first compartment in the 15 g/litre shock, and this was probably due to an increased fraction of the biomass being catabolically active due to higher bulk substrate concentrations enhancing mass transfer (Nachaiyasit, 1995). Inter- estingly, propionate always remained at concen- trations of less than 250 mg/litre, as with the 8 g/litre shock, and only increased slightly in compartment 2 (Fig. 11). Again, under shock loads the acetate/bu- tyrate ratios decreased to as low as 1.3 at hour 98. In compartment 2, all the glucose was consumed and the formate levels decreased to below 250 rag/ litre. High levels of acetate and butyrate were detected, and these could be the result of reduced levels of hydrogen which enhanced the conversion of short-chain fatty acid intermediates to acetate, but some of this acetate may have been converted to butyrate to keep acidity down since the ratio of acetate to butyrate was very low. In compartment 3 (data not shown) the acetate peak was around the same level as compartment 2 but appeared later. Butyrate in this compartment decreased from the levels in compartment 2, while propionate increased marginally, and hardly any formate was observed. Propionate persisted until the last compartment, with a slight decrease in each succeeding compartment, while acetate and butyrate decreased at a relatively higher rate, until only acetate was present in the last few compartments (Nachaiyasit, 1995). In conclusion, with a step increase in loading rate, the VFA "wave" moved down the reactor over time resulting in the "breakthrough" of VFAs in the diluent, and a decrease in COD removal. Reactor performance at steady state after the organic shocks A summary of reactor performance at steady state 20 days after the two organic shocks is shown in Table 1. The efficiency of COD removal was fairly constant at 98% when the feed concentration was doubled to 8 g/litre, but it showed a decrease to 90% when the feed concentration was increased to 15 g/litre due to the presence of VFAs which accounted for 1075 mg/litre COD of the 1530 mg/litre in the effluent. The methane yield (m3/kg-COD-de- stroyed) at 35 and 1 bar was 5-13% higher than the theoretical figure of 0.362 at both 4 and 8 g/litre, and this was probably due to errors in measuring the gas production rate over only 6 of the 24 h. However, at 15g/litre this figure was 20% higher than the theoretical, which, despite the stable COD results, may reveal that this reactor was not truly at steady state and that its long-term COD removal could increase to over 98%. Concluding discussion From the above data it can be seen that there are three general zones in the ABR: primarily acidifica- tion, active methanation and a buffer zone. As the loading rate increased, the buffer zone was used to absorb the overload and maintain the performance of the reactor until the loading rate was so high that it overloaded the system (the second shock load in this study), and VFAs consequently escaped into the effluent. In theory, given enough adaptation time, the slower growing methanogens could increase in number so that the performance of the ABR at high loads approached that of the baseline, and the methane yield data shows that the 15 g/litre reactor may not have been at steady state. It is noteworthy that formate did not seem to play an important role in these organic shocks. Grobicki and Stuckey (1991) found up to 2500 mg/litre of formate during a volumetric shock (hydraulic shock) load of 1-h HRT for 3 h. However, it appears that the results obtained in the present work tend to support the comment of Stams (1994) on the importance of hydrogen and formate as interspecies electron carriers that "formate might be more important than hydrogen transfer in suspended culture", since every time the results showed high levels of formate it was always coincident with high mixing conditions. These results show that the ABR is extremely stable to step organic shock loads and maintains the same removal efficiencies when the load is doubled instantaneously. When the feed strength is increased by a factor of 3.75 removal efficiency decreases slightly (98 to 90%), but the reactor coped with the shock well. The primary constituent of the COD in the effluent is unmetabolised VFAs which can be easily removed aerobically, and a small organic fraction which is SMPs. In contrast to earlier work with lower solids concentrations, the high solids used in this reactor resulted in enhanced stability to shock loads. It is apparent from the data that the unique compartmentalised structure of the ABR prevents most of the biomass being exposed to the low pHs encountered in the first few compartments during shock loads and, hence, enhances the stability of the reactor. The data obtained on the role of hydrogen and formate in interspecies electron transfer was some- what equivocal. Unlike earlier work, very little formate was detected in the reactor during shock loads, and this was contrary to what was expected, since no granules were observed in the reactor and, hence, the biomass was expected to be present as flocs. However, evidence from the use of recycle ABR shock loads: organic 2745 (Nachaiyasit and Stuckey, 1995) in this reactor has shown that, as the recycle ratio increases, with the concomitant increase in hydrodynamic mixing, there is an increase in formate production. Hence, it appears that bacterial associations in the biomass granules do partly determine the form in which the electrons are transferred between donors and acceptors. This effect may also have been due to the higher pHs in this work due to the higher alkalinity in the feed. The data also showed that hydrogen was a key intermediate and that hydrogen utilisers are present in the first compartment, where they produce considerable quantities of methane resulting in substantial COD reductions in the first compartment. McCarty and Mosey's (1991) hypothesis, formu- lated to predict VFA ratios under certain fermenta- tion conditions, suggests that, due to the low pHs and high substrate concentrations in the first compart- ment of the ABR during shock loads, the dominant group of bacteria would be the butyrate-forming bacteria which are obligate hydrogen producers (e.g. Clostridia). Some of these "butyric bacteria" have lost the ability to produce butyric acid and have become acetogens, producing only acetic acid, carbon dioxide and hydrogen; this maximises their energy yield, permitting faster growth. Others are acid-toler- ant bacteria that have retained the ability to produce butyric acid as a response to low pHs. These are in competition with the Propionibacteria, which can grow fast at high substrate concentrations and produce propionate/acetate/formate in fixed ratios but have a limited tolerance to low pHs and are poor scavengers (high substrate affinity coefficient). Low pH also inhibits the activity of the hydrogen scavenging methanogens and leads to the accumu- lation of hydrogen in the gas phase. Hence, this hypothesis appears to be able to explain the VFA ratios produced in the first compartment of the ABR under shock loads, which tend to consist of primarily acetic acid with increasing amounts of butyric acid over time, and a very low level of propionic acid, which is usually the most difficult VFA to remove after shock loads due to the low concentration of syntrophs and their very slow growth. This low rate of production of propionic acid in the ABR is one of the reasons that this reactor design is very stable to shock loads, and it is due primarily to its compartmentalised construction. CONCLUSIONS 1. The ABR is extremely stable at constant HRTs to step changes in feed COD, and it maintains high degrees of removal (>90%) weeks after a large shock. Hence, it would appear that the ABR would be appropriate for use in industry. 2. The compartmentalised structure of the ABR prevents much of the biomass being exposed to low pHs during step shock organic roads, and it maintains the biomass in the reactor for long CRTs. 3. Rapid fermentation of organic shock loads in the first compartment of the ABR lowers the pH and appears to result in the selection of a microbial population that produces primarily acetate and butyrate rather than propionate and formate. This results in a more stable response to shock loads, since both these acids are degraded relatively quickly in contrast to propionate. 4. Formate does not appear to be important as an electron acceptor during shock loads, in contrast to earlier findings, and this may be the result of different types of microbial flocs forming. head.ce:title: The effect of shock loads on the performance of an anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR). 1. Step changes in feed concentration at constant retention time

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A 10-litre anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR), with eight compartments, was used to examine the effect of organic shock loads, in the form of a step change in the feed chemical oxygen demand (COD) at constant hydraulic retention time (HRT), on reactor performance in terms of COD removal, and to obtain a greater insight into microbial responses and interactions during these shocks. In order to minimise feed variations, and have a totally biodegradable substrate, a synthetic carbohydrate (sucrose)-protein (meat extract) substrate was used. The reactor was operated at 20-h HRT, 4 g/litre COD (4.8 kg-COD/m3 d), and 35°C for 1 month as a base-line condition, and this resulted in 98% COD removal. It was found that a step change in the feed to 8 g/litre COD (9.6 kg-COD/m3 d) at 20-h HRT for 20 days did not affect the substrate removal efficiency at all; however, when the concentration was increased to 15 g/litre COD (18 kg-COD/m3 d) from 4 g/litre for 20 days, the removal efficiency decreased to 90%. It was found that the compartmentalised ABR consisted of three general zones (acidification, methanation, and a buffer zone where little acidification and methanogenesis occurs), and the function of high solids concentrations in the reactor was to enhance stability rather than improve COD removal. Hence, the structure of the ABR prevents most of the biomass being exposed to low pHs during shock loads, and enhances reactor stability. In addition, due to low pHs and high substrate concentrations in the first compartment, a microbial population seems to be selected which produces primarily acetate and butyrate rather than formate and propionate, and this also enhances the stability of the reactor during shock loads. In contrast to past results, formate did not seem to be an important interspecies electron carrier except under high mixing conditions and shock loads, and this was postulated to be due to differences in the structure of the microbial flocs. Based on these observations, the ABR holds some promise as a reactor design for anaerobic industrial wastewater treatment.
